sentences.sentence: Pronunciation: hye-DROX-ee-zeen Brand names: Vistaril (discontinued), Atarax (discontinued), generics available Dosage form: Hydroxyzine HCl tablets (10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg), Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules (25 mg), Hydroxyzine HCl oral solution (10 mg/5 mL) Drug classes: Antihistamines , Miscellaneous anxiolytics, sedatives and hypnotics
Medically reviewed by Melisa Puckey, BPharm .
Last updated on Sep 2, 2026.
Hydroxyzine is a prescription antihistamine used to treat anxiety and tension, itching from allergic skin conditions, and sedation before and after general anesthesia.
It comes in three oral forms:
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) tablets in 10 mg, 25 mg, and 50 mg strengths
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution (a syrup) containing 10 mg in each 5 mL
Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules in 25 mg
There is also a hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection.
It is given into a muscle by a healthcare professional and is never given into a vein or under the skin.
Hydroxyzine is not chemically related to benzodiazepines, phenothiazines, reserpine, or meprobamate.
Hydroxyzine taken by mouth is approved for three uses.
These are the same for hydroxyzine HCl and hydroxyzine pamoate.
Anxiety and tension.
For symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension linked to psychoneurosis, and as an add-on treatment in physical illnesses where anxiety is present.
Itching from allergic skin conditions.
For managing itching (pruritus) caused by allergic conditions such as long-term hives (chronic urticaria), eczema-type rashes, and rashes caused by contact with an irritant.
It is also used for itching caused by histamine release.
Sedation around surgery.
As a sedative given before a procedure (premedication) and after general anesthesia.
The injection is also approved for nausea and vomiting and is usually given in hospital or clinic settings.
It should not be used for nausea and vomiting caused by pregnancy.
Hydroxyzine has not been studied for long-term use in anxiety.
Studies have not assessed whether it still works as an anti-anxiety medicine beyond four months.
Your doctor should review from time to time whether you still need it.

Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain, below the outer layer known as the cortex.
It is not a cortical depressant, meaning it does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain the way some other sedatives do.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction.
This is what relieves itching.
Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle, widens the airways (bronchodilation), and reduces pain.
These are effects that have been observed rather than uses the medicine is approved for.
Hydroxyzine has also been shown to reduce nausea and vomiting.
This is an approved use for the injection, but not for the forms taken by mouth.
Take hydroxyzine exactly as your doctor prescribes.
Follow all directions on your prescription label.
Do not take more or less than prescribed, and do not take it for longer than your doctor tells you to.
Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how well you respond to treatment.
If you are taking the oral solution, measure your dose with the dosing syringe provided, a dose-measuring spoon, or a medicine cup.
Do not use a kitchen spoon, because it will not give an accurate dose.
Ask your pharmacist for a measuring device if you do not have one.
Call your doctor if your anxiety does not improve or if it gets worse.

sentences.sentence: If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness.
The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP).
Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin.
If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given.
In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects.
You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Weight gain is not among the side effects reported in FDA-approved labeling for hydroxyzine.
It does not appear in the labeling for the tablets, the oral solution, the pamoate capsules, or the injection.
This does not mean weight changes are impossible for every person.
If your weight changes while you are taking hydroxyzine, tell your doctor.
Do not take hydroxyzine if you:
are allergic to hydroxyzine or to any ingredient in the medicine
are allergic to cetirizine or levocetirizine
have a prolonged QT interval, a heart rhythm finding seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG)
are in early pregnancy
In animal studies, hydroxyzine caused birth defects in rats and mice at doses well above those used in people.
There is not enough information in humans to know whether hydroxyzine is safe in early pregnancy, so it should not be used at that time.

Hydroxyzine is not a controlled substance and has no DEA schedule.
This applies to both hydroxyzine hydrochloride and hydroxyzine pamoate.
Hydroxyzine makes the effects of central nervous system depressants stronger.
If you take hydroxyzine with any of the following, your doctor may need to lower the dose of the other medicine:
narcotic (opioid) pain medicines
non-narcotic pain medicines
barbiturates
Hydroxyzine may increase the effects of meperidine and barbiturates when used before anesthesia, so your doctor will adjust these doses for you individually.
Care is needed if you take other medicines that can affect heart rhythm by prolonging the QT interval.
These include:
heart rhythm medicines such as quinidine, procainamide, amiodarone, and sotalol
certain antipsychotics such as ziprasidone, iloperidone, clozapine, quetiapine, and chlorpromazine
certain antidepressants such as citalopram and fluoxetine
certain antibiotics such as azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin, gatifloxacin, and moxifloxacin
other medicines such as pentamidine, methadone, ondansetron, and droperidol
Hydroxyzine does not affect atropine or other belladonna alkaloids, and it is not known to interfere with digitalis.
It can be used at the same time as digitalis.
Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

Protect it from light and do not let it freeze.
Keep this and all medicines out of the reach of children.

Yes, hydroxyzine can be prescribed short term for anxiety and anxiety‑related trouble sleeping, usually as an “as‑needed” or bridging option rather than a long‑term daily medicine.
Evidence supports its short‑term anxiolytic and sedating effects, but its effectiveness and safety for chronic use beyond several months are not well established.

Hydroxyzine is intended for short-term anxiety treatment only, typically less than 4 months.
Long-term hydroxyzine use is considered off-label because no studies have examined the safety of extended use beyond this timeframe.
Some research suggests a link between long-term use of medications with anticholinergic properties, such as hydroxyzine, and dementia, particularly in older adults.
Brain fog has also been reported with long-term use.

Hydroxyzine’s noticeable calming and sedating effects typically last about 4–6 hours for most people, even though the drug itself stays in the body much longer due to an elimination half-life usually around 14–25 hours in adults and about 7 hours in children.

No, Benadryl does not treat anxiety, and in some people it can cause it.
Benadryl (diphenhydramine) is an allergy medicine that often makes people sleepy, so it may feel calming for a few hours.
But drowsiness is not the same as treating anxiety, and Benadryl is not FDA-approved for anxiety.

Hydroxyzine pamoate and hydroxyzine HCl both deliver the same active drug, hydroxyzine, so their clinical effects (such as sedation, itch relief, and anxiety reduction) are broadly similar.
The main difference is the salt form (pamoate vs hydrochloride), which influences how the medicine is formulated.

Hydroxyzine is not classified as a controlled substance in the United States, and current evidence does not show that it causes physical dependence or a characteristic withdrawal syndrome when stopped.
It is, however, a prescription-only sedating antihistamine that should be taken only under medical supervision.

Hydroxyzine and Benadryl (diphenhydramine) are both older, sedating H1 antihistamines, but they are different drugs with different FDA‑approved uses.
Hydroxyzine is available only by prescription in the United States, while diphenhydramine (Benadryl) is sold over the counter (OTC) in many allergy and sleep products.

Yes, dogs can take hydroxyzine.
Hydroxyzine is an antihistamine that may help treat allergies, anxiety, and motion sickness in dogs.
Hydroxyzine is not strongly linked to either weight gain or weight loss, and any changes in weight are usually mild and indirect rather than a direct effect of the drug.
In clinical studies, weight changes are uncommon and generally not considered clinically significant compared with other side effects such as drowsiness.
